conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like us to use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It simply helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me you’re in danger; then we’ll make a safety plan together. I’ll ask ten questions about the past seven days—no right or wrong answers, just whatever feels true for you. Ready to begin?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve noticed I don’t really laugh much anymore. Even when my partner tries to joke with me, it feels kind of forced if I crack a smile. It’s like the things that used to feel funny just don’t reach me right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… that hasn’t happened for me. I might manage a little smile, but actually laughing—like really laughing—hasn’t come easily at all this week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked—but lately it all feels flat. I still do them because I think I “should,” but that spark of looking forward to something just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right, or if I can’t get her settled quickly I’ll sit there replaying every little thing I did and convince myself it’s my fault. Even when my partner says “babies just cry,” I still feel like I’m failing somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay, or I’ll lie in bed hearing phantom cries even when she’s asleep. There’s this tight feeling in my chest that just shows up—no real reason, but I can’t shake it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s happened a few times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath, even if the baby’s fine and nothing’s going on. It passes after a bit, but in the moment it’s like my body thinks something terrible is about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get her down for a nap and the second I think I can breathe the laundry or dishes or a text I forgot to answer jumps out at me, and it’s like the walls close in. I manage, but it’s this constant sense of “how am I going to keep up?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… a few nights this week I’d lie down exhausted, but my mind just kept spinning—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying she’ll wake up any second. Even when she’s sleeping soundly, I can’t drift off; I end up staring at the ceiling for hours.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, that’s most days. There’s this heavy sadness that just sits on me. I’ll be holding the baby and tears start coming, and I can’t always tell you why—it just feels like I’m stuck under a gray cloud that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Once was when she wouldn’t stop crying and nothing I tried worked; I just sat in the rocker holding her, sobbing. Another time I was folding her tiny onesies and the tears started for no clear reason—just this wave of sadness that overflowed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ______________________

Symptoms / Behavioral Observations  
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, inability to experience pleasure (anhedonia)  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, episodic panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Pervasive self-blame and guilt re infant care, sense of maternal inadequacy  
- Sleep disruption secondary to ruminative worry, not solely infant demands  
- Overwhelmed by routine tasks, reports “treading water” most days  

Pattern  
Consistent endorsement of depressive and anxiety symptoms throughout 9/10 items; no self-harm ideation.

Risk Factors Identified  
- Postpartum onset within past 2–4 wks  
- Moderate–severe symptom intensity (multiple daily episodes)  
- Functional impairment: difficulty completing basic household/self-care tasks  
- Absence of protective factor: no enjoyment or support-seeking mentioned  
- Suicidality: Denied (Q10); no plan or intent

Screening Significance  
High clinical concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; warrants immediate formal evaluation and safety planning.
